# Quick reference {#sec-appendix-reference}

Every symbol in this book is decomposed piece by piece exactly once — in the chapter that owns it — and used freely ever after.
That discipline keeps the chapters readable, but it means a reader who skipped, or forgot, needs a map back to each symbol's home.
This appendix is that map, plus four more consolidations students asked for: an index of the recurring R idioms the code leans on, the football vocabulary the examples take for granted, a decision guide to the book's inferential catalog, and the complete ledger of the penalty convention's exhibits.
Nothing here is new; everything here is a pointer.

## Notation index {#sec-notation-index}

The table lists every piece of notation in the book, in the order the book introduces it, with a plain-words reading and the chapter where it is taken apart in full.

| Symbol | Read as | Introduced in |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------------------------|:--------|
| proportion (fraction / percent) | the share of cases with a given property, written as a fraction, decimal, or percent | @sec-data-hello |
| explanatory $\rightarrow$ response | the arrow of a suspected influence: explanatory variable might affect response variable | @sec-data-hello |
| association $\neq$ causation | two variables moving together does not mean one drives the other | @sec-data-hello |
| $\approx$ | approximately equal to | @sec-data-hello |
| $\bar{x}$ | "x-bar," the sample mean | @sec-explore-numerical |

| $\hat{p}_{sim}$ | the proportion from one simulated null-world sample | @sec-inference-one-prop |

| $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ | the difference between two sample proportions | @sec-inference-two-props |

| $\hat{p}_{pool}$ | the pooled proportion — all successes over all observations — used for the SE of a hypothesis test | @sec-inference-two-props |

| $T$ | the t-statistic | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| $t^\star_{df}$ | the critical value from a $t$-distribution with $df$ degrees of freedom | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| $df = n - 1$ | one-sample degrees of freedom | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| $SE = s / \sqrt{n}$ | the standard error of a sample mean | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| $SE_{BS}$ | the bootstrap standard error — the SD of the bootstrapped statistics | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| $\bar{x}_{bs}$ | the mean of one bootstrap resample | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ | the difference between two population means | @sec-inference-two-means |
| $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$ | the difference between two sample means | @sec-inference-two-means |
| $\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}$ | the two-sample SE for a difference in means | @sec-inference-two-means |
| $df = \min(n_1 - 1,\ n_2 - 1)$ | the conservative two-sample degrees of freedom | @sec-inference-two-means |
| $\mu_{diff}$ | the population mean of the paired differences | @sec-inference-paired-means |
| $\bar{x}_{diff}$ | the sample mean of the paired differences | @sec-inference-paired-means |
| $s_{diff}$ | the standard deviation of the paired differences | @sec-inference-paired-means |
| $n_{diff}$ | the number of pairs | @sec-inference-paired-means |
| $F$ | the F-statistic, MSG / MSE | @sec-inference-many-means |

| MSE | mean square error (within groups) | @sec-inference-many-means |

| $df_G = k - 1$ | group degrees of freedom, for $k$ groups | @sec-inference-many-means |
| $df_E = n - k$ | error degrees of freedom | @sec-inference-many-means |
| $SE_{b_i}$ | the standard error of a fitted regression coefficient | @sec-inf-model-slr |
| $t^\star_{n-2}$ | the critical value for a single-predictor slope | @sec-inf-model-slr |
| $b_i \pm t^\star SE_{b_i}$ | the confidence interval recipe for a coefficient | @sec-inf-model-slr |
| LINE conditions | Linearity, Independence, Normality (of residuals), Equal variability | @sec-inf-model-slr |
| $\varepsilon$ | "epsilon," the population error term around the true line | @sec-inf-model-slr |
| conditional $H_0\!: \beta_i = 0$ given others | a coefficient's null hypothesis, stated with the other predictors held in the model | @sec-inf-model-mlr |

## R idioms, indexed {#sec-r-idioms}

The code, like the notation, explains each construction only once — in the chapter that first needs it.
This table indexes the recurring idioms that are not self-evident from their names, with a plain-sentence reading and the chapter where each is first used and explained.

| Idiom | What it does, in one sentence | First used in |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:--------|
| **\|>** (the native pipe) | passes the result on its left into the function on its right, so a multi-step computation reads top to bottom | @sec-data-hello |
| `count()` then `pivot_wider()` | tallies rows by combinations of variables, then spreads one variable across the columns — the book's contingency-table builder | @sec-data-hello |
| `$` extraction | pulls a single column out of a data frame as a bare vector, ready for functions like `mean()` or `cor()` | @sec-data-hello |
| `%%` and `%/%` | remainder and whole-number division: `idx %% 10` cycles 0–9, `idx %/% 10` ticks up after every ten | @sec-explore-categorical |
| `\(x)` (a lambda) | defines a tiny anonymous function right where it is needed, instead of naming one elsewhere | @sec-explore-applications |
| patchwork's `+` and `/` | combines saved ggplots into one figure: `+` places side by side, `/` stacks vertically | @sec-model-slr |
| `map_dbl()` / `map_dfr()` with `reformulate()` and `set_names()` | applies a function to every element of a collection (returning numbers, or row-bound data frames), builds a model formula from strings, and labels a result vector — together, the machinery for fitting many candidate models at once | @sec-model-mlr (the stepwise-selection helpers); `map_dfr()` in @sec-foundations-mathematical |
| `replicate()` | runs the same expression many times and collects the results — the book's plainest simulation loop | @sec-foundations-bootstrapping |
| `after_stat()` | in a ggplot, refers to a quantity the plot computed (such as `density`) rather than a column of the data — how histograms get density-scaled for a normal-curve overlay | @sec-foundations-mathematical |
| `rep_slice_sample()` | infer's repeated sampler: draws many samples of a stated size, tagged by replicate number | @sec-foundations-applications |
| `droplevels()` | discards a factor's unused levels after filtering, so empty groups do not haunt later summaries | @sec-inference-many-means |
| the for-loop CV pattern | a `for` loop over folds: hold one fold out, fit on the rest, predict the held-out fold, accumulate the errors | @sec-inf-model-mlr, reused in @sec-inf-model-logistic |

: The book's recurring R idioms, in order of first appearance. {#tbl-r-idioms}

## The football, in one page {#sec-football-primer}

The examples assume no statistical background, but they do assume some football.
Here is every term the book uses without stopping to define it — in plain words, no diagram required.

**Penalty area.** The large box in front of each goal, 18 yards deep. Fouls by defenders inside it concede a penalty kick; most goals in the data are scored from inside it.

**Six-yard box.** The small box inside the penalty area, immediately in front of the goal. A shot arriving there is close-range by definition.

**Open play versus dead ball / set piece.** Open play is the game flowing freely. A dead ball is any restart after a stoppage — free kick, corner, penalty — and a set piece is the rehearsed routine a team runs from one. The book's datasets tag every shot with its origin, and the distinction carries the book's penalty convention (@sec-pens-at-a-glance).

**Cutback.** A pass pulled backward across the goal from near the byline to a teammate arriving in the box — one of the most reliable ways to create a high-quality shot.

**Low block.** A defensive strategy of retreating deep, packing players between the ball and the goal, and conceding territory but not chances. Morocco's 2022 run is the book's recurring example.

**Pressing.** The opposite instinct: hunting the ball high up the pitch, in coordinated groups, to force a turnover before the opponent can settle. The data's `under_pressure` tag marks shots taken while being closed down.

**Woodwork.** The goal frame — posts and crossbar. A shot off the woodwork that stays out counts as no goal, however close it came.

**Gilt-edged chance.** Scouting vernacular for an outstanding opportunity — the kind a striker is expected to score. Vague by design, which is why the book prefers a number (xG) to the phrase.

**Shot diet.** The mix of shots a team or player habitually takes — headers versus feet, close versus distant, open play versus set pieces. Two strikers with equal shot counts can have utterly different shot diets, and therefore utterly different conversion rates.

**Target forward.** A striker whose role is to receive long or crossed balls and finish close-range chances — typically few shots, high conversion: a walking confounder for naive comparisons.

**Rondo.** A training exercise — a circle of players keeping the ball from one or two defenders in the middle — that appears in the book's training-intervention scenarios.

**Per-90.** Normalization by playing time: a count divided by minutes played, times 90 (a full match), so that a starter and a substitute can be compared. Like any rate, it is treacherous on small denominators — a per-90 figure computed from 340 minutes is four matches of evidence wearing a season's confidence.

And the workplace the book drops you into, in two sentences: a scouting department runs a network of regional scouts who watch matches and file dossiers on prospects, which the club's analysts triage against data before shortlisting. The sporting director — Northbridge's Marta Vidal — makes the final sign-or-pass call, and your report is one of the inputs she stakes the budget on.

## Choosing a method {#sec-method-chooser}

Two questions locate almost every method in this book: *what is the response variable's structure*, and *do you want a test or an interval?*
The tables below consolidate the book's own recaps — @tbl-foundations-summary for the three inferential engines, and @tbl-zcompare / @tbl-tcompare for the mathematical catalog.
Remember that each mathematical row has simulation counterparts from the foundations chapters: a randomization test (@sec-foundations-randomization) wherever there is an explanatory variable to shuffle, and a bootstrap interval (@sec-foundations-bootstrapping) wherever there is a statistic to resample.

And before any row of any table applies, the book's standing reminder:

| First, always | |
|:------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| **Which observations are in the frame?** | State which shots (or players, or evaluations) the analysis includes and why, *before* computing anything. In this book's shot data that decision is usually penalties in or out — see @sec-chp11-pens-out and the ledger in @sec-pens-at-a-glance — and it has moved more verdicts than any formula. |

: The standing reminder that precedes every method choice. {#tbl-method-frame}

**Categorical response (z and chi-squared families).**

| Response | Question | Method | SE and df | Chapter |
|:----------------|:---------|:----------------------|:-----------------------|:-------|
| One proportion | Test vs $p_0$ | Z-test (success-failure with $p_0$); if it fails, simulate the null with `rbinom()` | $SE = \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}$ | @sec-inference-one-prop |
| One proportion | Interval | $\hat{p} \pm z^\star SE$; or bootstrap percentile | $SE = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$ | @sec-inference-one-prop, @sec-foundations-bootstrapping |
| Two proportions | Test of $p_1 = p_2$ | Z-test with *pooled* SE; or permutation test | $SE = \sqrt{\hat{p}_{pool}(1-\hat{p}_{pool})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}$ | @sec-inference-two-props |
| Two proportions | Interval for $p_1 - p_2$ | $(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^\star SE$ with *unpooled* SE | $SE = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$ | @sec-inference-two-props |
| Two-way table | Test of independence only (no single parameter, so no interval) | Chi-squared test, expected counts $\frac{\text{row} \times \text{col}}{n}$; or permutation | $df = (R-1)(C-1)$ | @sec-inference-tables |

: Method chooser for categorical responses. The test/interval SE substitution discipline ($p_0$ or pooled for tests, observed $\hat{p}$ for intervals) is @tbl-zcompare's. {#tbl-method-categorical}

**Numeric response (t and F families).**

| Response | Question | Method | SE and df | Chapter |
|:----------------|:---------|:----------------------|:-----------------------|:-------|
| One mean | Test vs $\mu_0$ | $T = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{SE}$ | $SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}},\ df = n - 1$ | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| One mean | Interval | $\bar{x} \pm t^\star_{df}\, SE$; or bootstrap | as above | @sec-inference-one-mean |
| Paired means | Either | Take each pair's difference, then run the one-mean row on the differences | $SE = \frac{s_{diff}}{\sqrt{n_{diff}}},\ df = n_{diff} - 1$ | @sec-inference-paired-means |
| Two independent means | Either | $T$ on $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$; interval $\pm\, t^\star SE$; or permutation / bootstrap | $SE = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}},\ df = \min(n_1 - 1, n_2 - 1)$ | @sec-inference-two-means |
| Many means ($k$ groups) | Test only (are *any* means different?) | ANOVA: $F = \frac{MSG}{MSE}$; or permutation of $F$ | $df_G = k - 1,\ df_E = n - k$ | @sec-inference-many-means |

: Method chooser for numeric responses, condensing @tbl-tcompare plus the ANOVA family. {#tbl-method-numeric}

**Model coefficients.**

| Response | Question | Method | SE and df | Chapter |
|:----------------|:---------|:----------------------|:-----------------------|:-------|
| Numeric (regression slope) | Test of $\beta_i = 0$ | $T = \frac{b_i}{SE_{b_i}}$; or permute the response | $df = n - 2$ (one predictor); software supplies $df$ with more | @sec-inf-model-slr, @sec-inf-model-mlr |
| Numeric (regression slope) | Interval | $b_i \pm t^\star_{df}\, SE_{b_i}$; or bootstrap | as above | @sec-inf-model-slr |
| Binary (logistic coefficient) | Test of $\beta_i = 0$ | Wald test, $Z = \frac{b_i}{SE(b_i)}$, against the standard normal | $SE(b_i)$ from software | @sec-inf-model-logistic |
| Binary (logistic coefficient) | Interval | $b_i \pm z^\star SE(b_i)$, back-transformed with $e^{(\cdot)}$ if odds are wanted | as above | @sec-inf-model-logistic |

: Method chooser for regression and logistic-regression coefficients. With multiple predictors, every hypothesis is conditional — "given the other variables in the model" (@sec-inf-model-mlr). {#tbl-method-models}

## The penalty convention at a glance {#sec-pens-at-a-glance}

Penalties — 64 at the 2022 World Cup, 51 at the 2025 Women's Euro, every one priced at 0.78 xG — sit on one side of most headline splits, so the frame decision (penalties in or out) can manufacture, mask, inflate, or flip a result all by itself.
The book's convention, set in @sec-chp11-pens-out, is to show every affected comparison both ways and treat the contrast as the lesson.
Here is the complete ledger of those exhibits, each recomputed in full in its owning chapter.

| Exhibit | Penalties in | Penalties out | What the penalties do | Where |
|:--------------------|:----------------|:----------------|:----------------|:------|
| Under-pressure conversion gap, permutation test (WC 2022) | $p = 0.084$ — discernible at $\alpha = 0.10$ | $p = 0.385$ — nowhere close | **Manufacture** a near-effect | @sec-chp11-pens-out |
| One-on-one conversion baseline $p_0$ (WC 2022) | $17/85 = 0.200$ | $17/77 = 0.221$ | **Drag the baseline down** — for once the artifact points the other way: all six 1v1 penalties were missed | @sec-inference-one-prop |
| Play pattern × goal table (WC 2022) | $X^2 = 162$ with the penalty row in | $X^2 = 4.63$, $p \approx 0.10$ | **Manufacture** a monstrous statistic | @sec-chp18-real-table |
| WEuro pressured mean xG vs WC benchmark | $T = -6.11$ vs $\mu_0 = 0.1259$ — thumping rejection | $T = -1.22$, $p = 0.22$ vs $\mu_0 = 0.0983$ | **Inflate the benchmark** the sample is tested against | @sec-one-mean-math |
| Pressured vs unpressured mean xG, two-sample (WC 2022) | $T = 4.27$, $p \approx 0.00003$ | $T = 0.37$, $p = 0.71$ | **Flip** the verdict | @sec-math2samp |
| Within-team paired pressure gap (WC 2022, 22 teams) | $T = -2.43$, $p = 0.024$ | $T = -0.28$, $p = 0.78$ | **Flip** the verdict — penalties can only sit on the unpressured side of a pair | @sec-mathpaired |
| Mean xG by position group, ANOVA (WC 2022) | $F = 6.10$ | $F = 12.30$ | **Mask**: the 0.78 spike doubles MSE and halves $F$ (both frames still reject) | @sec-mathANOVA |
| Single-mean xG benchmark, bootstrap 95% CIs (WC 2022) | $(0.1172,\ 0.1357)$ | $(0.0919,\ 0.1047)$ | **Inflate**: the two frames' intervals are disjoint | @sec-inference-applications |
| Wald test on the `one_on_one` coefficient, logistic model (WC 2022) | $b = 0.576$, $p = 0.074$ | $b = 1.126$, $p = 0.0005$ | **Flip** the verdict — six penalties carry the 1v1 tag | @sec-inf-model-logistic |
| The 1v1 premium on chance quality (WC 2022) | slope $0.127$ | slope $0.104$ | **Frame vs control**: removing six penalties moves the estimate the way analysts expect "controlling for" to — while actually adding controls moves it back up (to $0.1273$) | @sec-case-study-mario-cart |

: The book's penalty-convention exhibits, in chapter order. Every number is computed in the chapter cited. {#tbl-pens-at-a-glance}

Read down the fourth column and the moral assembles itself: the penalties' effect has no fixed direction — they have manufactured effects, masked them, inflated benchmarks, and flipped verdicts in both directions — which is precisely why no formula can absorb the frame decision for you.
State the frame, show both when it matters, and let the contrast teach.
